title: You start floating up and can't stop

narration.heading: Lift-off
narration.text: One morning you start floating straight up. And you can't stop.

narration.heading: 8.8 km up
narration.text: You pass Everest. The air is a third as thick here, and climbers call it the death zone.

narration.heading: 11 km up
narration.text: Airliners cruise here. Outside the window it's about minus 56 degrees.

narration.heading: 19 km up
narration.text: The Armstrong limit. The air is so thin that water boils at body temperature. Your spit would fizz.

narration.heading: 39 km up
narration.text: Felix Baumgartner jumped from here in 2012, and broke the speed of sound on the way down.

narration.heading: 100 km up
narration.text: The Kármán line. Most people count this as the edge of space.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: Up here the air can top a thousand degrees. But you'd still freeze. There's too little of it to heat you.

narration.heading: 400 km up
narration.text: You've reached the Space Station. It circles the whole Earth every 90 minutes.

narration.heading: Zoom out
narration.text: If Earth were an apple, all the air you just rose through would be thinner than its skin. How high would you go?

diagram.speed: The air = thinner than its skin

titles: What if you started floating up and couldn't stop?
Floating from the ground to the Space Station
youtube.description: One morning you start floating straight up. A 50-second rise past Everest, airliners, the Armstrong limit, Felix Baumgartner's record jump and the edge of space, all the way to the Space Station, and why the air up there is over 1,000 degrees but would still freeze you.

sources.claim: Everest is 8,849 m tall, with about a third of sea-level air pressure at the summit
Air at airliner cruising altitude (11 km) is about −56 °C in the standard atmosphere
The Armstrong limit (about 18–19 km), where water boils at body temperature
Felix Baumgartner jumped from 38,969 m on 14 October 2012 and reached Mach 1.25
The Kármán line at 100 km is the commonly used edge of space
The thermosphere can be extremely hot yet would feel very cold
The Space Station orbits about 400 km up, circling Earth about every 90 minutes
If Earth were an apple, the atmosphere would be as thick as its skin
